title: Oscillatory Haemodynamic Analysis During Venous-Return Interventions in Hyperacute and Early Acute Ischaemic Stroke: Secondary Analysis Protocol for the RETRAIN Phase 2 Randomized Trial (RR1-DE)
content: Background: In hyperacute and early acute ischaemic stroke interventions in clinical settings, functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) must be applied quickly by clinical staff. RETRAIN Phase 2 therefore recorded long-separation channels only. Short-separation (SS) channels, the usual reference for scalp and systemic haemodynamics, were omitted from the montage to allow rapid donning and doffing and because SS coupling through hair was unreliable in acute patients. Without SS channels, superficial and deeper-weighted contributions cannot be separated by standard regression. RETRAIN Phase 2 randomized adults with acute ischaemic stroke to common peroneal nerve neuromuscular electrical stimulation (CPN-NMES, geko™) or intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC). Its primary haemodynamic results have not been published, the primary manuscript is under review.Objective: To prespecify a secondary analysis of RETRAIN Phase 2 that applies a new, frozen long-channel-only method, coherence-volume-phase regression (CVP) with volume/flow indices and multichromophore operational modal analysis (OMA), to test the hypothesis that geko™ and IPC differ in superficial/systemic-weighted versus residual (deeper-weighted) haemodynamic response characteristics in hyperacute stroke. This Stage 1 Registered Report with Data Existing status (RR1-DE) does not concern the trial's primary outcome.Methods: The method was developed and tested without Phase 2 data. In two open fNIRS datasets with measured SS channels (OpenNeuro accession ds005776, n = 9-11 per task, Zenodo record 23163739, n = 22), with SS-regressed signals as the reference, and in RETRAIN Phase 1 recordings from 18 people with subacute stroke. Fifty-three Phase 2 participants were randomized (geko™ 27, IPC 26). Each session included a 5-minute device-off baseline and a 5-minute device-on period. Phase 2 will be analysed with paired Group x Period contrasts, participant-cluster bootstrap intervals, prespecified quality checks (including residual HbO-HbR coherence), comparator corrections (global signal regression, global-HbT regression, uncorrected signals) and null-simulation calibration.Results: Recruitment and data collection are complete (53 of 80 planned participants). No Phase 2 results have been published, the primary results manuscript is under review, and this protocol reports no Phase 2 estimates. In open data, CVP agreed better than global signal regression with SS-regressed HbR in all five test sets (e.g., Zenodo record 23163739 median r 0.88 vs 0.72) and null simulations showed that it does not create spurious HbO-HbR counterphase. In Phase 1, all indices were computable, and stimulation reduced residual HbO-HbR phase concordance (participant-level Δcos φ -0.16, 95% CI -0.28 to -0.05). Conclusions: This protocol tests whether long-channel-only fNIRS, compatible with rapid bedside application in hyperacute stroke, can separate superficial/systemic-weighted from residual responses well enough to compare two venous-return interventions. Results will be reported as estimates with explicit failure checks.
